interview_metadata.name: Nicole Lewis
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: Well, let me try to keep this organized. I was born in 1964 in Evanston, Illinois, and grew up in a quiet suburb just north of Chicago. My father was an electrical engineer at Motorola and my mother was a high school biology teacher, so our house was full of slide rules, lab notebooks, and a very particular sense of order — dinner at six, homework at seven, lights out at ten. I was an only child, which I think shaped my preference for solitude and structure. In high school I was the kid who color-coded her binders and ran the science club. I went to the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign and graduated in 1986 with a bachelor's in chemistry, and for a while I worked as a quality-control technician at a small pharmaceutical lab in Skokie. I met my husband Daniel at a Cubs game in 1989 — he was a high school math teacher at the time. We married in 1991 and settled in Morton Grove, where we still live. We tried for children for several years and weren't able to have them, which was a hard chapter, but we eventually made peace with it. In my forties I started caring for my mother as her dementia progressed, and that experience really redirected me — I left the lab work and went into home health as a personal care aide, because I'd seen firsthand what good and bad care look like. I've been doing that for almost fifteen years now, and I'm working toward a geriatric care management certification. So that's the arc — Midwest kid, science background, married, no children, second career in care.

follow_ups.question: What was your mother's dementia journey like for you?
follow_ups.response: It lasted about seven years. She was diagnosed in 2003 with early-onset Alzheimer's — she was only sixty-five — and I drove down to her place in Skokie three or four times a week after work. I kept a binder with her medications, her appointments, her behavioral notes. By the end she didn't know me, and that's a particular kind of grief. She passed in 2010. I think every care plan I write now has a little piece of her in it.

follow_ups.question: Why did the chemistry-to-caregiving switch make sense to you?
follow_ups.response: Honestly, the lab work was getting repetitive and I was watching aides come into Mom's house with no system, no documentation, no protocol. I thought, I can do this better — and I can bring the rigor with me. Vital signs are just data. Medication schedules are just spreadsheets. The skill set transfers more than people think.

follow_ups.question: How did you and Daniel decide to stop trying for children?
follow_ups.response: It wasn't a single conversation. It was more like a slow accumulation of disappointments over about four years, and then one Sunday in 1998 we were sitting on the back porch and Daniel just said, 'I think we're a family of two.' And I cried, and then I felt relieved, which surprised me. We got our first dog within a month.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: Yes, I'd say 2009 was that moment. My mother's care was consuming most of my evenings and weekends, and the lab where I worked offered me a senior QC supervisor position — more money, more hours, a real management track. At the same time, the home health agency that staffed Mom's aides offered me a part-time position because they were short-handed and they knew I was already doing the work informally. So there I was: a clear corporate ladder on one side, and on the other side an entry-level care job that paid less and had no obvious growth. I took about three weeks to decide. I made a spreadsheet — of course I did — comparing wages, benefits, hours, and what I called 'meaning index.' The lab job won on every financial metric. But I kept coming back to how I felt at the end of a shift caring for someone versus the end of a shift in the lab. I took the aide job in October 2009, and within a year I'd left the lab entirely.

follow_ups.question: Did Daniel weigh in on that decision?
follow_ups.response: He told me to follow the work that made me feel useful, and that we'd make the budget work. He's a teacher — he understood the calculus.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever regret it financially?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes when I look at our retirement projections I wince a little. But no, I don't regret the choice. The lab would have made me wealthier and a little hollow.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: Oh, it was very conscious. I had the spreadsheet, the pros-and-cons list, I talked to Daniel and to my pastor at the time. Nothing in my life 'just happens' if I can help it.

follow_ups.question: Is that true of most of your big decisions?
follow_ups.response: Yes. Daniel teases me that I planned our wedding like a NASA mission. Even our dog adoptions go through a checklist.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: I would have benefited from a career counselor who understood second careers in healthcare. The agency hired me on, but nobody really helped me think about credentialing or the long arc. I figured most of that out myself, years later.

follow_ups.question: Would a mentor have helped?
follow_ups.response: Tremendously. That's part of why I want to mentor new aides now — I want to be that person for someone else.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: My husband Daniel is the center of my family life. We've been married for thirty-five years this June. He retired from teaching high school math two years ago and now tutors a few students from home and volunteers at the library. We don't have children, as I mentioned, but we have a wonderful niece — Daniel's sister Karen has a daughter named Megan who just turned twenty-eight and lives in Madison. She calls me Aunt Nicole and we have a standing FaceTime on the first Sunday of each month. Karen and her husband Tom live in Glenview, about fifteen minutes away, and we do a family dinner with them every other Sunday — usually at our house because I like to cook. My father passed in 2017, eight years ago, of congestive heart failure. So my immediate inner circle is really Daniel, Karen and Tom, and Megan. And then our dog Winston, a seven-year-old beagle mix, who I would absolutely include in any family list.

follow_ups.question: What does a typical Sunday with Karen and Tom look like?
follow_ups.response: We aim for three o'clock. I usually do a roast chicken or a lasagna, Karen brings a salad, Tom brings wine. Daniel and Tom watch whatever game is on, Karen and I knit and gossip. We eat at five, they're out the door by seven thirty.

follow_ups.question: How do you and Daniel divide things at home?
follow_ups.response: He cooks breakfast on weekends and handles the cars and the lawn. I do the budget, the meals, the garden, and the dog's vet appointments. We split the cleaning.

follow_ups.question: Tell me more about Megan.
follow_ups.response: She's a public defender in Madison. Sharp as a tack, very mission-driven. I think I see myself in her in some ways — she likes systems and she likes helping people. She and her partner Jess came down for Easter.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: There's Daniel's brother Mark in Phoenix — we're cordial but not close. We exchange Christmas cards. That's about it for family I'd call immediate.

follow_ups.question: Do you see Mark in person?
follow_ups.response: Maybe every three or four years at a wedding or a funeral.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: My closest friend is Linda Petrowski — we've known each other since the early nineties when we both worked at the pharmaceutical lab. She lives in Park Ridge now. We have lunch every other Thursday at a little place called The Cottage. Then there's my knitting group — six women who meet at Three Bags Full yarn shop in Northbrook on Tuesday evenings. Bev, Gail, Marta, Ellen, Sue, and me. We've been together about nine years. I'm also close with Father James at Saint Martha's, and with Diane, who's the activity director at the senior center where I volunteer.

follow_ups.question: What does Tuesday knitting night look like?
follow_ups.response: We meet at six thirty, knit for two hours, drink decaf, and somebody always brings cookies. Gail brings the best lemon bars. We talk about everything — kids, husbands, politics in low voices, books.

follow_ups.question: How did you and Linda stay friends after you left the lab?
follow_ups.response: Honestly, deliberate calendar maintenance. We put the every-other-Thursday lunch on the books fifteen years ago and we just don't break it. Friendship at our age requires scheduling.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: We live in Morton Grove, in a quiet residential pocket near Harrer Park. It's an older suburb — our house was built in 1958 — and the neighborhood has a lot of mature oaks and maples. It's mixed: longtime homeowners like us, a growing number of younger families with kids, and a meaningful South Asian and Filipino community. The Metra line is about a mile away, and Daniel takes it into the city when he wants to go to the Art Institute. There's a Mariano's about two miles away where I do most of my grocery shopping, and a wonderful little farmer's market at the village hall on Saturday mornings from June through October.

follow_ups.question: How long have you and Daniel been in this house?
follow_ups.response: Twenty-eight years this fall. We bought it in 1997.

follow_ups.question: What's your block like?
follow_ups.response: Friendly but not nosy, which is exactly how I like it. We wave, we pick up each other's packages, we don't drop in unannounced.

follow_ups.question: Favorite spot in the neighborhood?
follow_ups.response: Harrer Park, hands down. Winston and I walk the perimeter loop every morning at six fifteen. There's a bench near the pond where I sometimes stop with my coffee.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: Very safe. I walk the dog before sunrise without a second thought. There was a string of car break-ins last summer on the next block, but that was unusual.

follow_ups.question: Do you lock up at night?
follow_ups.response: Always. That's just sensible, not fear.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: Mostly ups. The downside is the property taxes — they keep climbing — and the winters are punishing on my knees these days. But the stability and the proximity to my clients and family is worth it.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever considered moving?
follow_ups.response: Daniel floated Arizona a couple of years ago. I shut that down quickly. My whole life is here.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Just Daniel and me. And Winston the dog, who I count even though the census doesn't.

follow_ups.question: Always just the two of you?
follow_ups.response: Pretty much. My niece Megan lived with us one summer in college, but that was a long time ago.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone is permanent. Just Daniel and me.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Megan and her partner Jess stay over maybe three or four weekends a year. The guest room is always made up.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, no one.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Monday through Friday I work as a personal care aide. I'm up at five thirty, walk Winston by six fifteen, breakfast and shower, and out the door by seven thirty. I have three regular clients I see across the week — Mrs. Kowalski on Mondays and Wednesdays, Mr. Tanaka on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and a rotating Friday client. I'm usually home by four. Saturday is errands, the farmer's market, and my blueberry crumble afternoon ritual. Sunday is church at nine thirty, then either family dinner or a quiet day with Daniel and a crossword. Tuesday evenings are knitting group, Wednesday evenings are gentle yoga at the senior center, and Saturday mornings I usually do a birdwatching walk with the Audubon group.

follow_ups.question: What time does your day end?
follow_ups.response: Lights out at ten, almost without exception. Daniel sometimes stays up reading until eleven, but I'm rigid about my sleep.

follow_ups.question: Any day that breaks the pattern?
follow_ups.response: Rarely. If a client needs an extra visit or there's a family emergency. I plan my flexibility, if that makes sense.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I'm a personal care aide with Comfort at Home Services, a home health agency based in Skokie. I work weekday daytime hours, generally seven thirty to three thirty, sometimes four. With each client I do bathing assistance, dressing, medication reminders and administration where I'm permitted, light meal prep, vital sign monitoring, and detailed documentation in the agency's electronic health record. I also train new aides about once a month — the agency uses me as a sort of senior preceptor, though that's not officially my title yet.

follow_ups.question: What does the documentation piece look like?
follow_ups.response: I chart in the agency's system on a tablet at the end of each visit — vitals, medications administered, intake and output, behavioral observations. I'm probably the most thorough charter in the agency, which my supervisor appreciates and some of my coworkers find a little intimidating.

follow_ups.question: Tell me about training new aides.
follow_ups.response: I take a new hire on shadow shifts for two days, walk them through the EHR, demonstrate transfer techniques, and quiz them on medication safety. I built a one-page checklist that the agency has informally adopted.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I volunteer at the Morton Grove Senior Center on the first and third Saturdays of the month, helping Diane with the bingo and craft hours. I'm also the unofficial bookkeeper for our knitting group's yarn fund. And I tend a vegetable garden in our backyard from April through October — tomatoes, zucchini, basil, peppers, and a small herb bed.

follow_ups.question: Anything else?
follow_ups.response: I do my crossword every morning with breakfast — the New York Times Monday through Saturday, and the Sunday one I save for the afternoon. And Sudoku on the train when Daniel and I go into the city.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: Two changes. First, I started studying for my geriatric care management certification in January, so I block out an hour every weeknight from seven thirty to eight thirty for coursework. Second, my Friday client changed in March — my previous Friday client passed away, which was hard, and the new client is in Niles, which adds a fifteen-minute commute.

follow_ups.question: How are you handling the loss of your previous client?
follow_ups.response: Mr. Henderson. I cared for him for almost four years. I went to the funeral and I keep his thank-you card from last Christmas in my work bag. You learn to grieve and keep going in this work.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: We don't have children, so this doesn't apply to me. Though if it helps, my niece Megan is grown and works as a public defender in Madison.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: Very limited. A speeding ticket on I-94 about twelve years ago — I was going seventy-three in a sixty-five — and one minor fender-bender in a Mariano's parking lot where the Morton Grove police came out and were perfectly courteous. That's the extent of it.

follow_ups.question: How did the speeding ticket interaction go?
follow_ups.response: Polite, brief, deserved. I paid it that week.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: Through work I've called paramedics a number of times for clients, and police have responded a couple of times for welfare checks. Always professional in my experience.

follow_ups.question: Any specific incident?
follow_ups.response: Mrs. Kowalski had a fall last fall, I called 911, and the responders were excellent.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: No, no arrests in my immediate circle that I'm aware of.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote in every election. Federal, state, local, primaries, the school board races, the water reclamation district — all of it. I have a calendar reminder for the registration deadline before each cycle. Daniel and I usually vote early at the village hall together.

follow_ups.question: Why is voting important to you?
follow_ups.response: Civic responsibility, plain and simple. My parents took me to the polls with them as a kid. It's a habit I never broke.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I'd describe myself as a moderate Democrat with some pragmatic streaks. On healthcare I lean strongly progressive — I see the gaps in the system every single workday with my clients, and I support a stronger public option and better Medicare coverage for in-home care. On fiscal matters I'm more cautious; I budget at home and I think government should too, within reason. I'm pro-environment — birdwatching has made me a quiet conservationist — and I support sensible gun regulation. I'm a practicing Catholic and I have some complicated feelings on certain social issues, but on balance I think compassion and policy grounded in evidence should come first. I don't have patience for either party's extremes. I think a lot of our problems would be better solved by people who know how to read a spreadsheet and listen.

follow_ups.question: What issue would you want a candidate to address most?
follow_ups.response: Eldercare. The reimbursement structure for home health is broken, aides are underpaid, and the demographic wave is going to crash on us in the next decade.

follow_ups.question: Any politicians you particularly admire?
follow_ups.response: I had a lot of respect for Senator Dick Durbin and for the late John McCain — both for being willing to break with their parties when it mattered.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I've grown more progressive on healthcare and labor issues in the last decade — directly because of what I see at work. Aides are paid poorly, often without benefits, and turnover is brutal. Twenty years ago I might have said the market would sort it out; I no longer believe that. I've also become a little more skeptical of both parties' national leadership, though I still vote Democratic.

follow_ups.question: What's an issue you've changed your mind on?
follow_ups.response: Minimum wage. I used to worry it would hurt small businesses. Watching my coworkers struggle to pay rent on care wages changed that.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: Somewhat is honest. I'm a sixty-one-year-old white woman in a fairly diverse but mostly safe suburb, so the immediate impact on my life is limited. But I read closely, I followed the events of 2020 carefully, and I've thought a lot about how my Black coworkers and the Black families of some of my clients experience the world differently. The movement has made me more willing to listen and less willing to dismiss what I haven't personally seen.

follow_ups.question: Any specific reading or source that shaped your thinking?
follow_ups.response: I read 'The Warmth of Other Suns' by Isabel Wilkerson a few years ago. It changed how I think about Chicago itself, frankly.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the core grievance — that Black Americans face disproportionate harm in policing encounters — is well-documented and serious. I support better training, body cameras, and community accountability boards. I'm less comfortable with some of the more sweeping rhetoric, but I think the data is what it is.

follow_ups.question: How do you talk about this with friends?
follow_ups.response: Carefully. My knitting group has a range of views and we generally try to focus on facts when we discuss it at all.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think we've made real progress in my lifetime and I think we have substantial work left. Chicago's segregation patterns are still stark — you can drive thirty minutes and see two completely different cities. My parents' generation didn't talk about it openly; my generation talked about it sometimes; I hope my niece's generation is the one that actually moves the needle.

follow_ups.question: How does race come up in your work?
follow_ups.response: My agency and my clients are quite diverse. I've worked with Black, Filipino, Korean, and South Asian clients. Care doesn't have a color, but cultural humility absolutely matters in this job.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: Mostly conversations with Daniel and with Megan, who is much more activist than I am. I haven't joined protests — that's not my temperament — but I've donated to a couple of legal defense funds Megan suggested.

follow_ups.question: What did you donate to?
follow_ups.response: Megan pointed me to a Wisconsin public defender support fund. I gave a hundred dollars.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: Daniel is quietly progressive, like me. Megan is openly active — she's a public defender, this is her life's work. Linda, my best friend, is more conservative and we generally avoid the topic. My knitting group is mixed, leans moderate-to-liberal.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Generally good for sixty-one. I have mild osteoarthritis in both knees, which is why I do gentle yoga and walking instead of running. I take a low-dose statin for slightly elevated cholesterol — diagnosed in 2021 — and a daily multivitamin and vitamin D. My blood pressure runs 118 over 76, my last A1C was 5.4. I had a routine colonoscopy last fall, all clear. I get my annual physical with Dr. Patel at NorthShore every September.

follow_ups.question: Any other meds?
follow_ups.response: Just the statin — atorvastatin, twenty milligrams — and a low-dose aspirin Dr. Patel suggested. And I take melatonin maybe two nights a week if I can't fall asleep.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: Easy: structured routine, the dog who insists on walks, a husband who eats what I cook, garden vegetables in season, and good insurance through Daniel's retirement plan. Hard: my work involves a lot of physical lifting and bending, which is hard on the knees, and the emotional weight of caregiving accumulates.

follow_ups.question: How do you manage the emotional weight?
follow_ups.response: Yoga, knitting, time outdoors, and a frank conversation with Daniel when I need it.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Nothing dramatic. The arthritis flared last winter and I needed a cortisone shot in my right knee in February. Otherwise routine — annual physical, dental cleanings every six months, eye exam once a year for my reading glasses prescription.

follow_ups.question: How did the cortisone shot help?
follow_ups.response: Tremendously, for about four months. I'll probably need another one in the fall.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: Only minor — I had to take three days off work after the cortisone shot. The bigger long-term concern is whether my knees will let me keep doing direct care into my late sixties, which is part of why I'm pursuing the supervisory certification.

follow_ups.question: Have you discussed this transition timeline with anyone?
follow_ups.response: With Daniel and with my agency director, Janet. She's supportive.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Yes, my mother's Alzheimer's was the defining health caregiving experience of my life — she was diagnosed in 2003 and passed in 2010. My father had congestive heart failure for several years before he died in 2017, and I helped coordinate his care with a hospice team. Right now Daniel and I are both healthy, knock on wood.

follow_ups.question: How did caring for both parents shape you?
follow_ups.response: It made me ruthless about advance directives and family financial planning. We have everything documented.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: We've been fortunate — Daniel's teacher pension comes with very good retiree health coverage that I'm on as well. We haven't had to forgo care. There were some lean years in the early nineties when I delayed dental work, but nothing serious in the last twenty years.

follow_ups.question: How does your insurance situation compare to your coworkers?
follow_ups.response: I'm in the lucky minority. Several of my coworkers are uninsured or have only catastrophic coverage. It's one of the injustices of this industry.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Limited. I've done acupuncture twice for my knee — once in 2019, once in 2022 — and I found it modestly helpful. I take fish oil and turmeric. I'm skeptical of supplements that don't have evidence behind them, which is most of them. My STEM background makes me a hard sell.

follow_ups.question: What about meditation or mindfulness?
follow_ups.response: The yoga class includes some breathwork. That's about as far as I go.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I've never smoked. I drink moderately — a glass of red wine with dinner most evenings, maybe two on a Saturday. I've never used it as a coping mechanism in any concerning way.

follow_ups.question: What do you cope with instead?
follow_ups.response: Knitting, walking, the garden, a hot bath, talking to Daniel. Boring and effective.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: No marijuana, no recreational substances. The melatonin I mentioned is the only sleep aid I use, and that's intermittent. I took ibuprofen after the cortisone shot for a few days but I'm careful with NSAIDs given my age.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever tried marijuana?
follow_ups.response: Once in college, in 1984. Did nothing for me. Never tried it again.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: Through Daniel's retiree health plan, which covers both of us with reasonable copays. We have an HSA balance of about twelve thousand dollars that we maintained from his employed years. Out-of-pocket maximums are manageable on our budget.

follow_ups.question: Any concerns about the future?
follow_ups.response: Long-term care is the elephant in the room. We have a small long-term care insurance policy I bought in 2015. It's not enough.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: Strong supporter. I'm fully up to date — annual flu shot, Covid boosters, shingles, pneumococcal, the new RSV vaccine last fall. My job requires it and I'd do it anyway.

follow_ups.question: How do you handle vaccine-skeptical clients or family?
follow_ups.response: Patiently. I share what I know, I cite sources, I don't lecture. People come around at their own pace, or they don't.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: The CDC website, the Mayo Clinic, peer-reviewed journals when I can access them, and my own physician Dr. Patel. I also subscribe to a couple of geriatric care newsletters through my certification program.

follow_ups.question: Any podcasts or YouTube?
follow_ups.response: Not for medical information. I'm old-fashioned about sources.

transcript.question_text: Now we're going to talk a bit more about what life was like for you over the past year. Tell me all about how you have been feeling.
transcript.response: Generally steady. The big emotional event was losing Mr. Henderson, my Friday client of four years, in February. That hit harder than I expected. Otherwise it's been a year of forward motion — I started the certification coursework, Daniel and I took a wonderful trip to the Oregon Coast in September, the garden was the best it's ever been. I'd describe my baseline as calm and content with periodic dips that I weather well.

follow_ups.question: What does 'weather well' look like for you?
follow_ups.response: I let myself feel it for a defined period — a long walk, a good cry if needed — and then I get back to the routine. Routine is medicine for me.

transcript.question_text: Tell me a story about a time in the last year when you were in a rough place or struggling emotionally.
transcript.response: The week after Mr. Henderson died. The agency assigned the new Niles client right away and I was suddenly going to a strange house at a strange time, and I felt unmoored. I cried in the car twice that week. Daniel made me beef stew and we watched 'Schindler's List' on Sunday — which sounds counterintuitive but Spielberg's storytelling steadies me. By the second week I had my footing back.

follow_ups.question: Did you talk to anyone professionally?
follow_ups.response: No. I leaned on Daniel and on Father James. The agency offers an EAP but I didn't use it that time.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they struggle with depression, anxiety, or something else like that. How about for you?
transcript.response: I've never been formally diagnosed. I'd say I have a low-grade tendency toward anxiety that I manage through structure and routine — when my schedule is intact, I'm fine. When it's disrupted I notice a hum of worry. I had a brief course of talk therapy in 2011 after my mother died and it was very helpful. I'd consider it again if needed.

follow_ups.question: How do others describe your demeanor?
follow_ups.response: Calm. Unflappable, even. Most people don't see the worry hum because I don't let it leak out.

transcript.question_text: How has it been for your family?
transcript.response: Daniel had a rough patch right after retirement two years ago — the loss of identity that teachers often feel. He's settled into tutoring and library volunteering and is much better. Megan deals with secondary trauma from her caseload but she has a therapist she sees regularly.

transcript.question_text: Some people say that religion or spirituality is important in their lives, for others not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: Very important. I'm a practicing Roman Catholic. Daniel and I attend Saint Martha's parish in Morton Grove every Sunday at nine thirty mass — except in the deep winter when I sometimes do the Saturday vigil instead. Father James has been the pastor for about eleven years and I think very highly of him. I serve on the parish bereavement ministry, which sends meals and notes to families after a death in the community. My faith is more practice and community than doctrinal — I don't agree with the church on every social issue, but the rhythm of the liturgical year, the hymns, the people, all of that grounds me. I pray a short morning prayer most days and a rosary maybe once a month.

follow_ups.question: What do you most appreciate about Saint Martha's?
follow_ups.response: The music director is excellent and the bereavement ministry is one of the most active in the archdiocese. And it's diverse — we have Filipino, Polish, and Latino families all in the same pews.

follow_ups.question: Was Daniel raised Catholic too?
follow_ups.response: Yes, both of us — he's Polish Catholic on his father's side. We were married at his family's parish in Niles in 1991.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they use Facebook, Instagram, or other social media to stay connected with the wider world. How about for you? Tell me all about how you use these types of platforms.
transcript.response: I use Facebook lightly — mostly to keep up with the knitting group, a few cousins, and the parish. I check it maybe three times a week for ten minutes. I have an Instagram account I opened four years ago to follow the knitwear designer Stephen West and a few birding accounts; I post maybe once a month, usually a garden photo or a finished knit. I don't use Twitter or TikTok. Daniel doesn't use any of it.

follow_ups.question: Favorite Instagram follow?
follow_ups.response: Stephen West, hands down. His shawl patterns are my Everest.

follow_ups.question: Any platforms you've quit?
follow_ups.response: I had a Pinterest account briefly in 2018. It ate too much time.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they use Facebook or Twitter to get (emotional or financial) support during tough times. What about you?
transcript.response: Not really. My support comes from in-person relationships and the parish. Social media for me is a light hobby, not a lifeline.

follow_ups.question: Do you trust those platforms with personal stuff?
follow_ups.response: Not particularly. I keep my posts pretty surface — gardens, knits, the dog.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your level of stress, worry, and your emotional coping strategies.
transcript.response: Stress has been slightly elevated this spring because of the certification coursework on top of full-time work. I added a fifteen-minute meditation app session before bed about two months ago — Calm — and that's been helpful.

transcript.question_text: This might be repetitive, but before we go on to the next section, I want to quickly make sure I have this right: who are you living with right now?
transcript.response: Just my husband Daniel and our dog Winston. That's the household.

transcript.question_text: Any babies or small children?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Any lodgers, boarders, or employees who live here?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Who shares the responsibility for the rent, mortgage, or other household expenses?
transcript.response: Daniel and I share everything. The mortgage was paid off in 2019.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to talk about how you make ends meet and what the monthly budget looks like for you and your family. What were your biggest expenses last month?
transcript.response: Property taxes — we set aside about nine hundred dollars a month into a tax escrow we maintain ourselves. Then groceries, around six fifty. Utilities and insurance combined about five hundred. Health insurance premiums about three hundred fifty. The Oregon trip's last credit card bill was on there too — about eight hundred.

follow_ups.question: Any unexpected expenses?
follow_ups.response: Winston needed a dental cleaning — about four hundred dollars at the vet.

transcript.question_text: How much did your household spend in the past month? Is that the usual amount? And if not, how much do you usually spend and on what?
transcript.response: About fifty-two hundred last month, slightly above our typical forty-six hundred. I keep a detailed spreadsheet and we review it the first Sunday of every month.

transcript.question_text: Does your household own or rent your home?
transcript.response: We own. Bought in 1997 for one ninety-five, paid off in 2019. Current value somewhere around four-fifty.

transcript.question_text: Bills can fluctuate over the course of a year. Seasons change, there are holidays and special events, school starts and ends, and so on. Tell me all about how your bills have fluctuated over the past year.
transcript.response: Heating spikes in January and February — gas bill can hit two-fifty. December has the holiday gifts and parish donations. Summer brings garden supplies and the property tax installment. We took the Oregon trip in September which added about three thousand spread over two months. The certification program tuition was about fifteen hundred in January.

follow_ups.question: Anything coming up?
follow_ups.response: Property tax second installment due in August. We're already saving for it.

transcript.question_text: Tell me all about how you coped with any extra expenses in the past months.
transcript.response: We have a designated 'irregular expenses' line in the budget that funds itself at three hundred dollars a month. Most surprises come out of that. The Oregon trip was funded from a separate travel sub-account.

transcript.question_text: Some people have a savings account, some people save in a different way, and some people say they don't save. How about you?
transcript.response: We save consistently. Daniel has his teacher pension which provides a base monthly income. We have a Vanguard IRA we both contribute to, an HSA, a high-yield savings account at Ally for the emergency fund, and a small brokerage account with a target-date 2030 fund. The emergency fund is at six months of expenses.

follow_ups.question: Who manages the investments?
follow_ups.response: I do, with input from a fee-only advisor we see annually. I find investing soothing — it's basically a giant spreadsheet.

transcript.question_text: Some people save for big things, like a home, while others save for a rainy day. How about for you (in the last year)?
transcript.response: Both. We're building toward a more comfortable retirement around when I turn sixty-seven, and we maintain the emergency fund. Specific goals include the Kyoto trip we'd like to take for our fortieth anniversary in 2031 — I have a sub-account for that with about forty-two hundred saved so far.

transcript.question_text: Some people have student loans or credit card debt. Others take out loans from family or friends or find other ways of borrowing money. Tell me about all the debts you're paying on right now.
transcript.response: None. Mortgage is paid off, no student loans — we paid those off years ago — and we pay credit cards in full every month. We have one Chase Sapphire card we use for everything to get the points.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any time during the past year that you haven't had enough money to buy something that you needed or pay a bill that was due.
transcript.response: Hasn't happened in many years. We're fortunate, and we've been disciplined.

transcript.question_text: What is or was your occupation? In this occupation, what kind of work do you do and what are the most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: I'm a personal care aide with Comfort at Home Services. My core duties are: assisting clients with activities of daily living such as bathing, dressing, grooming, and toileting; medication reminders and administration where state regulations permit; meal preparation according to dietary plans; vital signs monitoring and documentation; safe transfer and mobility assistance; light housekeeping; and detailed charting in the agency's EHR. I also do new-aide training and serve as an unofficial preceptor.

follow_ups.question: Most important skill?
follow_ups.response: Observation. The aide who notices the small change — slight gait difference, slight cognitive change — prevents the big crisis.

transcript.question_text: Was your occupation covered by a union or employee association contract?
transcript.response: No. The agency is non-union. There's been some quiet talk about organizing in the home health sector regionally but nothing at our agency.

transcript.question_text: In the past year, how many weeks did you work (for a few hours, including paid vacation, paid sick leave, and military service)?
transcript.response: Fifty weeks. I took two weeks off — one for the Oregon trip, one around Christmas.

transcript.question_text: How many hours each week did you usually work?
transcript.response: Thirty-five to thirty-eight, depending on client schedules.

transcript.question_text: In the past week, did you work for pay (even for 1 hour) at a job or business?
transcript.response: Yes, thirty-six hours this past week.

transcript.question_text: Did you have more than one job or business, including part time, evening, or weekend work?
transcript.response: Just the one job at Comfort at Home Services. The training I do is part of the same role.

transcript.question_text: Now, in the past month, how many jobs did you work, including part time, evening, or weekend work?
transcript.response: One.

transcript.question_text: For your job or occupations, how much money did you receive in the past month?
transcript.response: About thirty-two hundred dollars net. My hourly is twenty-three fifty plus a small training stipend when I onboard new aides.

transcript.question_text: How often do you get paid?
transcript.response: Biweekly, direct deposit on Fridays.

transcript.question_text: In total, how much did your household make in the past month?
transcript.response: Roughly seventy-five hundred. My thirty-two hundred plus Daniel's pension of about thirty-eight hundred plus his tutoring income of about five hundred.

transcript.question_text: Switching gears a bit, let's talk a little about tax time. Did you file taxes last year (the most recent year)?
transcript.response: Yes. We file jointly. I prepare everything in TurboTax and our accountant Margaret reviews it before we file. We filed by March 15 this year.

transcript.question_text: Tell me more about your workplace. How long have you been at your current job? How would you describe the benefits that come with your job? (This could include things like health benefits, paid time off, vacation, and sick time.)
transcript.response: Almost fifteen years at Comfort at Home Services. Benefits are modest — two weeks PTO accrued, a small 401(k) match up to three percent, and a partial health stipend that I don't use because I'm on Daniel's plan. No paid sick leave separately; it comes out of PTO.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your relationships at work? (How is your relationship with your manager or boss? How are your relationships with your coworkers?)
transcript.response: Excellent with my supervisor Janet, who's run the agency for twenty years and has championed me for the supervisory track. Cordial with most coworkers, close with two — Maria, who's been there almost as long as me, and Kayla, a younger aide I've trained and mentored.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about how predictable your work schedule is. How would you describe your job in terms of flexibility with your hours?
transcript.response: Very predictable for our industry — I have established weekly client assignments and the agency respects that I prefer not to take last-minute fill-in shifts. I get my schedule for the week on Friday afternoons. Flexibility is decent if I need a personal day, less flexible day-to-day because clients depend on punctuality.

transcript.question_text: Some people say it's hard to take or keep a job because of child care. How about for you?
transcript.response: Not applicable — we don't have children.

transcript.question_text: Do you receive any payments or benefits from SNAP, food stamps, housing voucher payments, supplemental security income, or any other programs like that?
transcript.response: No, none of those.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about times over the last year when your income was especially low. And tell me about all the things you did to make ends meet during that time.
transcript.response: No really lean months in the past year. December was lighter on hours because of the holiday week off, but Daniel's pension is steady so it didn't affect us materially.

transcript.question_text: What would it be like for you if you had to spend $400 for an emergency? Would you have the money, and if not, how would you get it?
transcript.response: Easily. The emergency fund covers six months of expenses. I'd just transfer it from Ally.

transcript.question_text: Overall, how do you feel about your financial situation?
transcript.response: Stable and grateful. Not wealthy by any modern standard, but secure. The paid-off house and Daniel's pension are the two pillars. My main worry is long-term care costs in our late seventies and eighties — the long-term care insurance we bought won't be sufficient if both of us need significant care simultaneously. But for now, I sleep well.

transcript.question_text: Are you now married, widowed, divorced, separated, or have you never been married? If you are not currently married, are you currently living with a romantic partner?
transcript.response: Married, currently living with my husband Daniel. Thirty-five years this June.

Were you born in the United States? If you were not born in the U.S., what country were you born, and what year did you first come to the U.S. to live?
transcript.response: Yes, born in the U.S.

transcript.question_text: What city and state were you born in?
transcript.response: Evanston, Illinois.

transcript.question_text: Are you of Hispanic, Latinx, or Spanish origin?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: What race or races do you identify with?
transcript.response: White.

transcript.question_text: What is the highest degree or grade you've completed?
transcript.response: Bachelor's degree, chemistry, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, 1986.

transcript.question_text: Are you enrolled in school?
transcript.response: I'm enrolled in a geriatric care management certification program, online through a continuing education provider. Not a degree program.

transcript.question_text: Have you been enrolled in school during the past 3 months?
transcript.response: Yes, since January in the certification program.

transcript.question_text: Have you ever served on active duty in the U.S. Armed Forces, Reserves, or National Guard?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: What religion do you identify with, if any?
transcript.response: Roman Catholic.

transcript.question_text: Generally speaking, do you usually think of yourself as a Democrat, a Republican, an Independent, or what? And how strongly do you associate with that party?
transcript.response: Democrat. Moderately strongly — I'm not a registered party activist, but I've voted Democratic in every general election since 1988 with one exception in a local race. I'd say I'm a moderate-to-liberal Democrat.

transcript.question_text: Do you think of yourself as closer to the Democratic Party or to the Republican Party?
transcript.response: Democratic, clearly.

transcript.question_text: What was the city and state that you lived in when you were 16 years old?
transcript.response: Skokie, Illinois. We moved from Evanston to Skokie when I was twelve.

transcript.question_text: Did you live with both your own mother and father when you were 16?
transcript.response: Yes, both.

transcript.question_text: Who else did you live with?
transcript.response: No one else. I was an only child.

transcript.question_text: What's the highest degree or grade your dad completed?
transcript.response: Master's degree in electrical engineering.

transcript.question_text: What's the highest degree or grade your mom completed?
transcript.response: Bachelor's degree in biology, with a teaching certificate.

transcript.question_text: Did your mom work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, she worked throughout my childhood.

transcript.question_text: What was her job? What kind of work did she do? What were her most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: She was a high school biology teacher at Niles West High School. She taught freshman biology and AP Biology, ran the science club, and was the department chair for several years in the late seventies.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did she work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where she worked?
transcript.response: Niles Township High School District 219, a public school district. A large suburban high school.

transcript.question_text: Did your dad work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, the entire time.

transcript.question_text: What was his job? What kind of work did he do? What were his most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: Electrical engineer at Motorola in Schaumburg. He worked on semiconductor design — I never fully understood the specifics. He led a small engineering team in the eighties.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: Motorola — at the time a large American electronics and semiconductor company. They made everything from two-way radios to early cell phones.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: I hope to finish my certification in the next eighteen months and step into a supervisory role at the agency by sixty-three or sixty-four. I want to design a standardized care workflow that other agencies might adopt. I want Daniel and me to be healthy enough to take that Kyoto trip in 2031 for our fortieth anniversary. I hope our garden keeps producing, our dog has a long life, and Megan continues to thrive. I hope I get to mentor at least a dozen new aides into long careers. And I hope, when our time comes, that we have our affairs so well-organized that no one has to puzzle over anything.

follow_ups.question: Anything you hope to be different?
follow_ups.response: I'd like to feel I've left a fingerprint on how home care is done in this region. The big pieces of life are settled — the legacy is what's still in motion.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: Daniel, first. The marriage. After that: dignity in care — both giving it and someday receiving it. Order, in the sense that systems and routines free people up to focus on what matters. And the small daily pleasures — the morning walk with Winston, the first tomato of August, a finished shawl, a quiet mass on a Sunday morning. Those are the things.

summaries.behavioral_economist: Nicole exhibits a strong preference for structure, planning, and pre-commitment: a documented monthly budget reviewed every first Sunday, named savings sub-accounts (emergency fund at 6 months expenses, Kyoto trip fund at $4.2K, irregular-expenses line at $300/mo), no consumer debt, and a Chase Sapphire card paid in full for points optimization (Q56-Q63, Q83). Major decisions are made via spreadsheets and pros/cons lists — she explicitly recounts using one to weigh the 2009 career pivot from a higher-paying lab role to home health aide work (Q02, Q03), suggesting she values intrinsic 'meaning' and consistency over financial return when both are above a comfort threshold. Her risk tolerance is low but informed: she carries long-term care insurance, sees a fee-only advisor annually, and worries about long-term care underinsurance despite strong baseline finances (Q40, Q61, Q83). Habits are sticky and ritualized (6:15 am dog walk, Saturday blueberry crumble, biweekly knitting group of 9 years, every-other-Thursday lunch of 15 years), indicating high present-bias resistance and strong identity-based consumption (Q07, Q08, Q15).
summaries.political_scientist: Nicole is a high-information, high-participation moderate Democrat: she votes in every federal, state, local, and primary election with calendar-reminder discipline (Q23, Q95, Q96). Her politics are pragmatically left-of-center and shifted progressive over the last decade specifically on healthcare, eldercare, and labor policy as a function of direct occupational exposure to home health workforce conditions, suggesting an experiential rather than ideological updating mechanism (Q24, Q25). She names Senator Durbin and the late Senator McCain as figures she respects, signaling preference for institutionalist, cross-aisle politicians (Q24). Civic engagement is consistent but quiet — she donates modestly to causes (e.g., $100 to a Wisconsin public defender fund) and avoids protests, channeling civic identity through her Catholic parish ministry and senior center volunteering rather than partisan activism (Q17, Q29, Q47). Institutional trust is high for the CDC, Mayo Clinic, peer-reviewed science, and her physician (Q42).
summaries.psychologist: Nicole presents as high-conscientiousness, moderate-to-high-introversion, low-neuroticism on the surface with a self-described 'low-grade anxiety hum' she manages structurally rather than affectively (Q03, Q15, Q45). Her self-concept is built around being orderly, observant, and dependable; she leverages routines, lists, and spreadsheets as primary self-regulation tools and considers them 'medicine' (Q43, Q45). Coping strategies are healthy and varied — exercise (yoga, walking), creative absorption (knitting, gardening, crosswords), spiritual practice (Catholic mass, rosary, parish community), social connection (long-term scheduled friendships), and brief past use of talk therapy after her mother's 2010 death (Q38, Q44, Q45, Q47). Relationally she is warm but selective, investing deeply in a small set of bonds (husband, niece, best friend, knitting group) and tolerating distance with peripheral kin like brother-in-law Mark; her motivational architecture centers on competence, service, and legacy — finishing the certification, mentoring aides, and 'leaving a fingerprint' on regional home care while keeping a private fear of late-life caregiving needs (Q05, Q06, Q07, Q83, Q108).
